h1: The 6 Best Transfer Boards of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 transfer boards compared on length, stated weight capacity, material and turntable or slide-sheet design for beds and cars.
summary: The DMI Transfer Board 30 x 8 x 1 is the best all-round board: Scotch pine, two cutout handles, tapered ends and a stated 440 lb capacity. The shorter DMI 24 inch suits tight gaps, the King Mills XXL is the wide wooden option, and the Sienson and LOSCHEN turntable boards help users who struggle to pivot with a caregiver present.
intro: Most transfer board buying mistakes are about length, not strength. A board that spans the gap with no margin tips as soon as weight lands near one end, and a board that is far too long hangs off a wheelchair seat and blocks the armrest. The correct length depends on the two surfaces involved, which is why the same person may need one board for the bed and another for the car.

We compared six boards on stated length, width, capacity and material, then split them into plain boards and turntable designs. We make no medical claims: a transfer board is a mobility aid, and a clinician or occupational therapist should confirm technique and sizing. Where a listing leaves capacity vague, we mark it as a risk, because weight limits are the one spec you should never assume.

products.name: DMI Transfer Board 30 x 8 x 1, Cutout Handles
products.verdict: A 30 inch Scotch pine board with a stated 440 lb capacity, two cutout handles and tapered ends.
products.description:
DMI's board is the reference design: 30 inches long, 8 wide and 1 thick, cut from sanded and sealed Scotch pine, with a stated 440 lb capacity. Two cutout handles give a caregiver a grip for positioning, and tapered ends let the board slide under a user or onto a seat edge without a hard step.

It ranks first because it combines a high stated limit with the most common length. The 24 inch DMI is lighter but shorter, and the turntable boards lower the stated capacity or leave it unstated. The tradeoff is the surface: bare wood is a plain slide, which suits users who can push themselves but not those who struggle to rotate.

Best for users and caregivers who want a proven board with a high stated limit. The caveat is that wood is not as hygienic as plastic, so wipe it down after use.
products.idealFor: Users and caregivers who want a proven, no-frills wooden board with a high stated limit.
products.skipIf: The user struggles to pivot and needs a turntable.

products.name: DMI Transfer Board 24 Inch, Cutout Handles
products.verdict: A 24 inch, 8 inch wide Scotch pine board with the same stated 440 lb capacity, under $25.
products.description:
This DMI is the 24 inch version of the longer board, 8 inches wide, in Scotch pine with two cutout handles and the same stated 440 lb capacity. It is listed as an FSA item, and it falls in the under $25 bracket.

It ranks second because shorter boards suit a narrower set of transfers: wheelchair to a nearby chair, or bed to a chair parked right against it. For gaps wider than the board, it is unsafe, which is why the 30 inch version ranks above. What you gain is portability and lighter weight, which caregivers lifting it in and out of a car appreciate.

Best for short, close gaps. The caveat is that you should measure the gap before buying, because a board that barely spans it tilts under load.
products.idealFor: People with a short, close gap who want a lighter wooden board that stores easily.
products.skipIf: The gap between surfaces is wide.

products.name: King Mills Pinewood Plus Size Transfer Board XXL
products.verdict: A wider, longer pinewood board rated to 300 lb with two cutout handholds and a 1 year warranty.
products.description:
King Mills built this XXL board wider and longer than standard sizes for larger users, from real pinewood with two cutout handholds. It is rated to 300 lb and carries a 1 year warranty, which is a rarity in this category. The extra width gives more surface to bear weight across the transfer.

It ranks third because the 300 lb rating is lower than the DMI boards' stated 440 lb, even though it is the plus-size option. The listing does not publish exact dimensions in its specs, so measure carefully. Against the turntable boards, it is simpler and cheaper to operate, but it provides no rotation assistance.

Best for users who need extra width and are within the rated limit. The caveat is that the rating is a hard ceiling, not a suggestion.

products.name: Sienson Turntable Slide Board, 35.4 Inch
products.verdict: A 35.4 inch ABS board with a 360 degree turntable and a 330 lb stated capacity.
products.description:
Sienson's board stretches 35.4 inches, which spans the wider gaps between a car seat and a wheelchair. An ABS plastic body carries a rotating disc with an EVA anti-slip pad, a 360 degree turntable, and a grid anti-slip pattern underneath. Stated capacity is 330 lb (150 kg).

It ranks fourth because a turntable adds complexity and a lower stated limit than the 440 lb DMI boards. The upside is the pivot: the user sits on the disc and rotates, rather than sliding, which suits those who struggle to shift their hips. Against the LOSCHEN, it is longer and publishes a capacity.

Best for car and van transfers. The caveat is that rotating discs reduce friction in every direction, so a trained caregiver should handle the first transfers.
products.idealFor: Wider gaps, such as a car or van seat, where a long board with a turntable is needed.
products.skipIf: The user needs the highest stated capacity.

products.name: LOSCHEN Transfer Board with Turntable, 29.5 Inch
products.verdict: A 29.5 x 8.9 inch ABS board with a 12 inch rotating disc. Caregiver assistance required.
products.description:
LOSCHEN measures 29.5 by 8.9 by 0.9 inches in ABS plastic, with a 12 inch rotating disc that turns 360 degrees. The listing states plainly that caregiver assistance is required, which is the right framing for a device that changes how weight moves.

It ranks fifth because the listing does not give a capacity figure in the specs we reviewed, and weight limits are the first thing to confirm on a transfer board. Against the Sienson, it is shorter but similarly designed, and its 0.9 inch thickness is slimmer than the 1 inch wood boards, which makes it easier to slip beneath.

Best for households with a trained caregiver. The caveat is the missing capacity figure: do not buy until you have confirmed it with the seller.
products.idealFor: Households where a trained caregiver assists a user who struggles to pivot.
products.skipIf: You need a confirmed weight limit before buying.

products.name: suboton Transfer Board with Slide Sheet, 31.5 Inch
products.verdict: A 31.5 x 8 inch board bundled with a 28 x 28 inch slide sheet, three handles and curved edges.
products.description:
suboton bundles a 31.5 by 8 inch board with a 28 by 28 inch green slide sheet, three handles, curved edges and an anti-slip underside. The sheet reduces friction when repositioning a person in bed, and the extra handle helps a caregiver control the board.

It ranks last because the listing does not clearly state a weight capacity, so the bundle's value is hard to trust. Against the DMI boards, which publish a 440 lb limit, this one asks you to confirm the rating first. The package is attractive, though: sheet and board in one purchase from the $50 to $100 bracket.

Best for caregivers who need both a board and a slide sheet. The caveat is that you should verify capacity with the seller before use.
products.idealFor: Caregivers who want a board and slide sheet in one package and will confirm the capacity first.
products.skipIf: You need a published weight limit.

whatMatters.detail: Capacity is the maximum load the manufacturer says the board carries. The DMI lists 440 lb, the Sienson 330 lb and the King Mills 300 lb. Never exceed it, and be cautious with listings that give none. Compare the number with the user's weight plus a safety margin.

The board must bridge the gap with several inches resting on each surface. A 24 inch board suits close, level transfers, while a car or van often needs 30 inches or more. Measure the distance between the two seats, including any armrest or door sill.

A plain board lets the user slide across, while a turntable lets them rotate in place. Turntables can help users with limited hip mobility but add a moving part. Check whether the listing says caregiver assistance is required, as the LOSCHEN does.

Sealed wood is rigid and familiar, and the DMI uses sanded Scotch pine. ABS plastic wipes clean and is lighter. Look for sanded edges, a sealed finish and anti-slip features, and avoid any board with cracks or splinters.

Cutout handles let a caregiver steady and move the board, while tapered or curved edges help it slide under a user. Check the number of handles, and confirm the underside is anti-slip, because a board that shifts mid-transfer is the commonest hazard.

faq.q: How do I know what length of transfer board I need?
faq.a: Measure the gap between the two surfaces and add several inches resting on each. The DMI 24 inch suits close chairs, the DMI 30 inch handles most beds, and the Sienson 35.4 inch spans wider car gaps.

faq.q: What is the biggest transfer board mistake?
faq.a: Ignoring the weight limit. The King Mills is rated to 300 lb and the Sienson to 330 lb, below the DMI's 440 lb. Check the stated capacity and leave margin.

faq.q: Is a turntable board worth it over a plain board?
faq.a: Only if the user struggles to pivot and a trained caregiver assists. The Sienson and LOSCHEN rotate, but both add a moving part. A plain DMI board is simpler and carries a higher stated capacity.

faq.q: How do I use a transfer board safely?
faq.a: Lock wheelchair brakes, set the board firmly on both surfaces and move in small steps. Ask an occupational therapist to demonstrate the method. The LOSCHEN listing explicitly says caregiver assistance is required.

faq.q: How do I clean a transfer board?
faq.a: Wipe wooden boards like the DMI with a damp cloth and dry them fully, since sealed pine can still absorb moisture. ABS boards such as the Sienson can be wiped with mild disinfectant.

faq.q: Can I use a transfer board in a car?
faq.a: Yes, with the right length. The Sienson is built for wider gaps like car seats. Park on level ground, open the door fully, and have a caregiver steady the board.

finalTake: For most users the DMI Transfer Board 30 x 8 x 1 is the right board: sealed Scotch pine, cutout handles, tapered ends and a stated 440 lb capacity. Choose the shorter DMI for tight gaps, the King Mills for a wider surface, and the Sienson when a trained caregiver needs a turntable for car transfers.
